blocks.text: Jordan is compact enough to see a surprising amount without spending half the trip on the road. Petra is the main reason many people come, but with a few more days you can sleep in Wadi Rum, spend time at the Dead Sea, visit Jerash and Amman, or continue south to Aqaba.

Our Jordan Tours range from 3 to 9 days. A shorter trip can concentrate on Petra and a few nearby stops, while a week gives you much more room to travel from northern Jordan through the Dead Sea area and Petra to Wadi Rum. Depending on the itinerary, arrangements can include hotels, airport transfers, private transportation, guided sightseeing with licensed local guides, and local support during your trip. Private Tours and Customized Tours are available for travelers who want to adjust the route or pace.

One of the advantages of travelling in Jordan is that the experience changes quickly from place to place. Roman ruins in Jerash, the stone façades of Petra, the open desert of Wadi Rum, and the Dead Sea can all be part of the same journey without needing domestic flights between them.

sections.heading: Petra: How Much Time Do You Need?

blocks.text: Petra deserves more time than a quick walk to the Treasury and back. You enter through the Siq, but beyond the Treasury the site continues through tombs, temples, Roman remains, and trails leading to viewpoints and the Monastery.
On shorter Jordan itineraries, Petra naturally takes up a large part of the trip. If you have more time, an additional night gives you a less rushed visit before continuing south to Wadi Rum.

The change from Petra to Wadi Rum is one of the most interesting parts of travelling through Jordan. Within a few hours, archaeological sites give way to open desert, sandstone formations, and long stretches of almost empty landscape.

Wadi Rum is usually explored by 4x4 with a local Bedouin driver. Some itineraries continue onward the same day, while others include a night in a desert camp. If Aqaba is part of the trip, it fits naturally after Wadi Rum rather than requiring a separate detour.

sections.heading: The Dead Sea, Madaba & Mount Nebo

blocks.text: These three stops work well together geographically. Madaba is known for its mosaics, including the Byzantine map of the Holy Land, while nearby Mount Nebo looks across the Jordan Valley and has a long biblical association.

The Dead Sea can then be included as a sightseeing stop or an overnight stay. How long you spend there depends largely on whether you want some downtime at a resort or simply want to experience the water before continuing the journey.

Amman is often treated simply as the arrival point, but the Citadel and Roman Theatre make it worth including in the itinerary. North of the capital, Jerash has extensive Roman-era streets, temples, theatres, and public spaces that can be explored on foot.
With additional time, the route can continue farther north to Umm Qais. On a shorter trip, Jerash is the easier addition before heading south.

sections.heading: How Many Days Should You Allow for Jordan?

blocks.text: Three or four days can work if Petra is your priority, but there will inevitably be compromises. With five or six days, it becomes much easier to include Wadi Rum and the Dead Sea without treating every stop as a quick visit.

Seven days or more gives you room to include northern Jordan, Madaba and Mount Nebo, or Aqaba, depending on what interests you. Because most of the route is travelled overland, adding another night often improves the pace rather than simply adding another destination.

Spring and autumn are popular for Jordan because temperatures are generally easier for walking around Petra, Jerash, and Wadi Rum. These are also busy periods, particularly at the country's best-known sites.

Winter is cooler and can be quite cold at night in Petra and Wadi Rum. Summer is much hotter, especially around the Dead Sea and southern Jordan, so sightseeing times need a little more thought. Aqaba has its own warmer Red Sea climate and can be included at different times of year.

sections.heading: Jordan on Its Own or with Another Country?

blocks.text: Jordan does not need to be an extension to another trip. With a week available, there is enough to build a varied itinerary entirely within the country.
If you are already travelling in the region, however, Jordan can also be combined with Turkey or Egypt. See our Turkey & Jordan Vacation Packages or Jordan & Egypt Tours for existing combinations.
For longer regional itineraries, our Multi Country Tours include routes connecting Jordan with additional destinations.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for a Jordan tour?
faqs.a: Most first-time visitors need five to seven days to explore Amman, Jerash, Petra, Wadi Rum, and the Dead Sea at a comfortable pace. Eight or nine days allows time for Aqaba, Madaba, Mount Nebo, additional Petra sightseeing, or a longer resort stay. Three- or four-day packages focus mainly on Petra and Amman.

faqs.q: What is the best Jordan itinerary for first-time visitors?
faqs.a: A well-balanced first-time itinerary normally includes Amman, Jerash, Madaba, Mount Nebo, Petra, Wadi Rum, and the Dead Sea. Seven days provides enough time to experience these destinations without excessive rushing. Travelers with eight or nine days can also add Aqaba, northern Jordan, a second Petra day, or more relaxation.

faqs.q: Is Petra worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes. Petra is one of the world’s most important archaeological destinations and offers far more than the famous Treasury. Visitors enter through the dramatic Siq and can explore royal tombs, temples, churches, theaters, colonnaded streets, hiking trails, and the Monastery. A full day is recommended for most first-time visitors.

faqs.q: Is one day enough to visit Petra?
faqs.a: One full day is sufficient to walk through the Siq, see the Treasury, and explore the main archaeological route. However, two days are preferable for travelers who want to visit the Monastery, Royal Tombs, High Place of Sacrifice, or additional hiking trails without rushing. The best duration depends on fitness and interests.

faqs.q: How much walking is required in Petra?
faqs.a: A standard Petra visit normally involves several kilometers of walking over stone, gravel, and uneven surfaces. Reaching the Treasury requires walking through the Siq, while the Monastery involves approximately 800 steps. Travelers with mobility limitations can follow a shorter route, but most of Petra is not fully wheelchair accessible.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Wadi Rum?
faqs.a: Yes. An overnight stay in Wadi Rum is one of Jordan’s most memorable experiences. Camps range from traditional Bedouin-style tents to premium dome accommodation with private bathrooms. Most overnight programs include dinner, breakfast, sunset views, and stargazing. Camp facilities, heating, air conditioning, and meal arrangements should be confirmed before booking.

faqs.q: What is included in a Wadi Rum jeep safari?
faqs.a: A standard Wadi Rum jeep safari generally includes transportation in a four-wheel-drive vehicle operated by a local Bedouin driver. The route may visit rock formations, canyons, natural arches, viewpoints, and ancient inscriptions. Safari duration varies by itinerary, so travelers should confirm whether the program includes two, four, or more hours.

faqs.q: Is the Dead Sea worth including in a Jordan tour?
faqs.a: Yes. The Dead Sea offers a distinctive floating experience, mineral-rich mud, resort facilities, spa treatments, and dramatic landscapes. A short stop is sufficient for travelers with limited time, but an overnight resort stay provides a more relaxing experience. It works particularly well after the walking and desert activities in Petra and Wadi Rum.

faqs.q: Should I visit Aqaba during my Jordan trip?
faqs.a: Aqaba is worth adding when you have at least seven or eight days and want beaches, snorkeling, diving, resort accommodation, or relaxation after Petra and Wadi Rum. It is especially suitable for families, couples, and divers. Travelers focused entirely on archaeology may prefer additional time in Petra, Amman, or northern Jordan.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year to visit Jordan?
faqs.a: March through May and September through November usually provide the most comfortable conditions for Petra, Wadi Rum, Amman, and the Dead Sea. Summers can be very hot, particularly in desert regions, while winter brings cooler days and cold desert nights. Jordan remains visitable year-round when itineraries are planned appropriately.

faqs.q: Are Jordan tours private or group based?
faqs.a: Magnificent Travel offers Private Tours, Small Group Tours, and fully Customized Tours. Private programs provide greater flexibility, private transportation, and a schedule tailored to your preferences. Small Group Tours follow more structured routes and may share selected services. The exact service type, guide arrangements, and group size are stated in each proposal.

faqs.q: Can Jordan tours be customized?
faqs.a: Yes. Jordan Tours can be customized according to your travel dates, hotel category, preferred pace, interests, and available time. You may add a second Petra day, upgrade your Wadi Rum camp, extend the Dead Sea stay, include Aqaba, visit northern Jordan, or combine Jordan with Turkey, Greece, Egypt, or Israel.

faqs.q: Are licensed guides included in Jordan tour packages?
faqs.a: Licensed local guides are included when specifically listed in the confirmed itinerary. Some Jordan programs use an experienced English-speaking driver between destinations and licensed local guides at major archaeological sites. Guiding arrangements differ according to itinerary length, group size, and package type, so the exact services should be reviewed before booking.

faqs.q: Is the Jordan Pass worth buying?
faqs.a: The Jordan Pass is often worthwhile for eligible travelers visiting Petra and several included attractions. It offers one, two, or three consecutive Petra entry days and may waive tourist visa fees when the required stay conditions are satisfied. Its value depends on nationality, entry point, itinerary, and the number of included sites visited.

faqs.q: Do I need a visa to visit Jordan?
faqs.a: Visa requirements depend on nationality, passport type, entry point, length of stay, and current Jordanian regulations. Many nationalities may qualify for a visa on arrival or an electronic visa, while others require advance arrangements. Travelers should verify current requirements through the relevant Jordanian authority or diplomatic mission before departure.

faqs.q: Is Jordan safe for organized tours?
faqs.a: Jordan’s main tourism destinations receive international visitors throughout the year, but regional conditions and official travel advice can change. Travelers should review current government guidance before departure and follow local instructions. A professionally organized tour provides coordinated transportation, reliable local contacts, planned routes, and assistance if operational changes become necessary.

faqs.q: Is Jordan suitable for families with children?
faqs.a: Jordan can be highly rewarding for families when daily schedules balance archaeological sightseeing with rest and enjoyable activities. Children often enjoy Petra, Wadi Rum jeep safaris, desert camps, floating in the Dead Sea, and Aqaba. Private Tours are particularly practical because walking time, breaks, hotel choices, and departure times can be adjusted.

faqs.q: Is Jordan suitable for senior travelers?
faqs.a: Yes. Jordan can be planned for senior travelers through private transportation, carefully selected hotels, shorter walking routes, and a relaxed schedule. Petra requires the greatest physical effort, although the Siq and Treasury area may suit many visitors. Mobility requirements, room access, dietary needs, and medical considerations should be discussed before confirmation.

faqs.q: What should I wear while traveling in Jordan?
faqs.a: Lightweight, breathable, and modest clothing is suitable for most Jordan tours. Shoulders and knees should generally be covered when visiting religious sites or traditional communities. Comfortable walking shoes are essential for Petra and archaeological areas. Bring sun protection in warmer months and warm layers for winter evenings and Wadi Rum nights.

faqs.q: Are meals included in Jordan tour packages?
faqs.a: Daily breakfast is commonly included at hotels, while Wadi Rum camp stays may include dinner and breakfast. Lunches and additional dinners are included only when stated in the itinerary. Package arrangements vary, so travelers should review the confirmed inclusions and advise the tour operator in advance about allergies, dietary restrictions, or special meal requirements.

faqs.q: How do travelers get around Jordan?
faqs.a: Most Jordan itineraries use private air-conditioned road vehicles because the principal destinations are connected by highway and domestic flights are generally unnecessary. Private transportation provides flexibility for sightseeing stops and luggage. Driving times vary, particularly when using the scenic King’s Highway instead of the faster Desert Highway between Amman and Petra.

faqs.q: Can Jordan be combined with Egypt?
faqs.a: Yes. Jordan and Egypt combine particularly well in a ten- to fifteen-day itinerary. Travelers can explore Cairo, the Pyramids, Luxor, Aswan, or a Nile Cruise before flying to Amman for Petra, Wadi Rum, and the Dead Sea. Regional flights, hotels, transfers, and sightseeing can be coordinated through one itinerary.

faqs.q: Can Jordan be combined with Turkey?
faqs.a: Yes. Turkey and Jordan Tours can combine Istanbul, Cappadocia, Petra, Wadi Rum, Amman, and the Dead Sea in approximately nine to fourteen days. Longer itineraries may also include Ephesus and Pamukkale. Flights between Turkey and Jordan, domestic transportation, hotels, transfers, and local guides can be professionally coordinated.

faqs.q: Can Jordan be combined with Greece?
faqs.a: Yes. Greece and Jordan Tours combine Athens, selected Greek islands, Petra, Wadi Rum, Amman, and the Dead Sea. Most combined journeys require approximately nine to fourteen days, depending on the number of islands and Jordan destinations selected. Flight schedules, ferries, transfers, hotels, and sightseeing should be planned together.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I book a Jordan tour?
faqs.a: Booking three to six months in advance is recommended for spring and autumn, particularly around Easter, public holidays, and other busy travel periods. Early booking provides a better selection of Petra hotels, Dead Sea resorts, Wadi Rum camps, private guides, and regional flights. Last-minute arrangements may offer less flexibility.

faqs.q: Are international flights included in Jordan tour packages?
faqs.a: International flights are included only when specifically stated in the itinerary and quotation. Standard Jordan-only packages normally begin and end at an agreed airport or border point, while Multi Country Tours may include selected regional flights. Travelers should check baggage allowances, ticket conditions, schedules, and included sectors before confirming the package.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a traditional and luxury Wadi Rum camp?
faqs.a: Traditional camps generally provide simpler tents, shared or basic facilities, local meals, and a more rustic desert experience. Luxury camps may offer private bathrooms, heating, air conditioning, upgraded bedding, panoramic windows, or dome accommodation. Standards vary considerably, so room type, facilities, location, meals, and cancellation terms should be confirmed carefully.
